Convex supports and convolution cancellation

Reconstructed and checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A convolution can lose isolated points of support through complex cancellation. For two compact distributions its convex hull is nevertheless exactly the sum of the two factor hulls. We prove the statement in every dimension, including its approximation steps, and then determine when actual support can be recovered.

The dimension is fixed. Pairings are complex linear and . Write , and let denote compactly supported distributions. The convolution lesson, B0–B3 and Theorems 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 3.2 and 5.2, proves support localization, tensor products, convolution under proper addition, smoothing, associativity, joint weak sequence convergence on fixed supports and shrinking approximate identities. Finite point jets and their independence are proved in angular foundations, A3. The ordinary integral operations, finite-dimensional compactness and scalar calculus used below have the exact supplied proof locations listed at the end.

Positivity, affine confinement and differential operators

Proposition 4.1. Let be positive locally finite Borel measures, with at least one compactly supported. Then their convolution is a locally finite positive measure and Proof. Addition is proper on the two supports: if the first is compact and the output lies in a compact , the second coordinate lies in , also compact. The product integral of is consequently finite for compactly supported bounded ; it defines the convolution measure by the product measure and is positive. Its support has the usual upper inclusion. The sum of the supports is closed: for a convergent sequence , compactness gives a subsequence , whence in the other closed support.

For the lower inclusion, take support points and an open neighborhood of . Choose small relatively compact open balls about them whose closure sum is contained in . A nonnegative smooth cutoff supported in equals one on this compact sum. Both and are positive by the definition of measure support, and finite by local finiteness. Thus . Every such detects the convolution. If either measure is zero, both sides of (4.1) are empty.

Proof. Group the monomials of according to which variables have positive exponent; this proves existence and uniqueness of (4.3). The fundamental theorem applied to gives . Tensor differentiation therefore yields These terms give all stated upper inclusions. If , the distribution equals the nonzero constant on the open square, so support closedness fills . If and , in a neighborhood of any relative interior point of a vertical edge the only nonzero term is the normal point jet times the nonzero interval density in . Independence of point jets supplies a normal test with nonzero pairing; a tangential nonnegative test of positive integral completes a detecting tensor test. These facts prove all cases.

Solution 8. The difference of two compact solutions is annihilated by the nonzero compact kernel ; Corollary 4.2 makes the difference zero. A solution for must itself be nonzero. Let and . Theorem 3.1 gives .

For a nonempty compact , its directional width is . This is the maximum of minus its minimum, so it is nonnegative. Applying the support-sum identity yields For , this last width is strictly positive: if it were zero, all three scalar products would equal zero, so would be perpendicular to the basis , a contradiction. A nonempty compact set in an affine line has zero width in a nonzero normal direction. Thus a line-supported cannot admit a compact solution. The inequality is a necessary condition; the argument makes no assertion of sufficiency.

Programme proof locations and freely accessible sources

  • Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B3 and Theorems 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 3.2, 5.2: localization, tensors, proper convolution, support inclusion, smoothness, associativity, joint limits on fixed supports and normalized mollifiers. These are the exact earlier proofs used throughout Sections 2–4 and the solutions.
  • Angular foundations, A3: independence of arbitrary finite point jets, used in Corollary 4.3, Proposition 4.4 and Solution 7.
  • Schwartz and Fourier foundations, F3: the full real Gaussian mass proof used in (3.5)–(3.6).
  • Metric foundations, §§12–13: finite-dimensional compactness, completeness of the real numbers, scalar fundamental theorem, exponential series and smooth cutoffs. Stable algebra foundations, §10: finite-dimensional linear algebra and determinants. Banach foundations, §§15.1–15.3, 16.1–16.2: dominated convergence, Fubini–Tonelli, Cauchy–Schwarz, linear changes of variables and product measures.
